sections.h2: Who records deeds and mortgages in Peoria County?
sections.html:
The Peoria County Clerk's office runs land records for the county, and its Land Records page is the starting point for deed recording, the property index, transfer declarations and the fee schedule. The office is in the courthouse at 324 Main Street, Room 101, Peoria, IL 61602, and answers the phone at (309) 672-6060 Monday through Friday, from half past eight in the morning to half past four

The county's land records site lets you search the index, but the county itself warns that the index works like a library card catalogue. It points to a document and should not be relied on to decide anything about the underlying paper. Pull the recorded deed itself, or ask the title company for the chain of title, before you rely on a name or a legal description.

sections.h2: How does e-recording work in Peoria County?
sections.html:
Peoria County accepts documents electronically from approved submitters, and the e-Recording page lists two: Indecomm Global Services and Simplifile. Title companies, lenders and law firms use that route, and the county says documents are usually recorded and returned within 24 hours instead of weeks or days.

  • It saves postage and removes the race to the courthouse counter on closing day.
  • Rejections are fewer and corrections come back faster than on paper.

Documents that do not come through one of those submitters go to the Clerk's office on paper, so ask the closer which route your sale will use.

sections.h2: What forms go with a deed in Peoria County?
sections.html:
Every deed needs the Illinois Real Estate Transfer Declaration, form PTAX-203. Peoria County takes part in the state MyDec system, so the declaration can be filed electronically before the deed is recorded. Under the state's description, buyer and seller fill out the form together and file it in the property's home county.

Deeds for land inside the city of Peoria carry extra paperwork. The table lists what the county and city pages describe.

sections.h2: How much is transfer tax on a Peoria County sale?
sections.html:
Illinois charges a state transfer tax and lets counties add their own, and home rule cities can add another. The Department of Revenue tells readers to use its Tax Rate Database for the state figure and says counties may impose 25 cents per $500 of value. The county recorder collects the tax by selling revenue stamps that the county buys from the state.

The City of Peoria sets its own tax at $2.50 for each $1,000 of value, or fraction of $1,000, stated on the transfer declaration, under an ordinance passed in 1989. The city's instruction sheet says the payment is made at the county recording office. If the home stays subject to an existing mortgage, the state notes that only the owner's equity counts toward the tax base when the deed says so on its face. Ask your closer for the stamp total before signing, since it depends on the stated value.

sections.h2: What are the recording fees in Peoria County?
sections.html:
The Peoria County Clerk's Land Records page links a current fee schedule and a predictable fees notice. The county has posted a notice that fees increase on January 1, 2027. Ask the Clerk or your closer for the per-page and per-document amounts in force on your recording date, since a deed recorded in December and one recorded in January may be priced differently.

The page also carries a link to predictable fees information. Check both before you hand a deed to a courier, because the Clerk's totals add up from several line items.

sections.h2: What other protections does the Peoria County Clerk offer owners?
sections.html:
The Land Records page lists a Fraud Guard service described as a simple way to avoid becoming a victim of property fraud. It also describes the Illinois Anti-Predatory Lending program and GIS maps that anyone can download as PDFs. Owners who rarely look at their parcel record, such as heirs or landlords out of town, should read what the county says about each of these.

Taxes that have been sold are also handled here. The default redemption period is two years from the sale, a tax buyer may extend it to three, and the minimum for a home of one to six units is two and a half years. Payment must come as a cashier's check, money order or cash made out to the Peoria County Clerk, with no personal, mortgage or title company checks. Ask the title company to build the redemption amount into the payoff.

sections.h2: How does a deed recording connect to the Peoria County tax bill?
sections.html:
The tax bill follows the parcel number, not the person, and the Treasurer prints a single bill for each parcel. For 2025 taxes the county planned to mail bills by May 1, 2026, with installments due June 9 and September 9. The Treasurer says a missing bill does not excuse payment, and asks owners who have none by May 15 to call the office.

The County Clerk also extends the rate for each taxing district and says current levy, valuation and rate information is posted by May 15 each year. A tax district search on the county site returns your district by address. Parcel details and bill history are available at propertytax.peoriacounty.gov, and both offices can confirm whether a sale year still carries sold taxes before your closing date.

sections.h2: What do Peoria County numbers say about the local housing market?
sections.html:
QuickFacts estimates 178,553 residents for July 2025, down 1.9% from the 2020 base, in 84,884 housing units. About 67.0% of homes are owner-occupied, the median owner-occupied value for 2020-2024 is $158,500, and median gross rent is $993. Median household income is $65,108.

  • Peoria County covers 618.73 square miles of land with about 293.9 people per square mile.
  • Of residents age 25 or older, 34.9% hold a bachelor's degree or higher.
  • Workers average 19.2 minutes of travel to their jobs.
  • The county counts 4,168 employer establishments for 2023.

A deed that moves a house in the county's central city lands in a city where renters make up a larger share than in the county as a whole, which matters if a tenant occupies the home at closing.

faqs.q: Where do I record a deed in Peoria County?
faqs.a: With the Peoria County Clerk at 324 Main Street, Room 101, in Peoria. Hours run from half past eight to half past four on weekdays, and the phone number is (309) 672-6060. Title companies and law firms can send deeds electronically through Simplifile or Indecomm Global Services.

faqs.q: Do I need a transfer declaration for a deed in Peoria County?
faqs.a: Yes. Form PTAX-203, the Illinois Real Estate Transfer Declaration, goes with the deed, and Peoria County allows electronic filing through MyDec. Land inside the city of Peoria also needs the city's own declaration and, for certain transfers, an exemption certificate.

faqs.q: What is the City of Peoria transfer tax rate?
faqs.a: The city's instruction sheet prints $2.50 for each $1,000 of value or fraction of $1,000 stated on the declaration. The payment is made at the county recording office, and commercial or multi-family transfers also need a current zoning certificate from City Hall.

faqs.q: Are Peoria County recording fees changing?
faqs.a: Yes. The county posted a notice of a fee increase on January 1, 2027. The Clerk's Land Records page links the current schedule, and the Clerk can quote the amount for your document type and page count before you submit it.

faqs.q: Can I redeem sold taxes at the Peoria County recorder's office?
faqs.a: Yes. Redemption of sold taxes is handled by the County Clerk, in one payment of cash, a cashier's check or a money order payable to the Peoria County Clerk. Partial payments and payment plans are not allowed, and an online estimate of redemption shows the next penalty date.
